subject: political-science
part: Part III · The European Union as a Political System
readings: Bulmer, Parker, Bache, George & Burns (2020) ch. 19, "The Single Market" · Jensen & Nedergaard (2012), "From 'Frankenstein' to 'toothless vampire'?"

cards.front: What makes a market genuinely **"single"** rather than a mere **free-trade area** or **customs union**?
cards.back:
A **single market** doesn't stop at removing **tariffs** — it attacks the **hidden barriers** that survive after tariffs are gone (different standards, licences, service rules, qualifications, tax/admin systems).

**Goal:** remove the extra cost created *simply by crossing a border*, so **27 sovereign states** with different laws and regulators trade as **one market**.

Built on **free movement + removal of barriers + common rules where necessary.**
cards.hint: More than the absence of tariffs.

cards.front: Name the concept: **national regulations, product standards, licences, admin requirements and discriminatory practices that impede trade even after tariffs and quotas are gone.**
cards.back:
**Non-tariff barriers (NTBs).**

They sit above two easier layers — **tariffs** (largely removed inside the customs union) and **quantitative restrictions / quotas** (prohibited). NTBs are **much harder to remove** — *this is the real work of the single market.*

★ The hard part of integration **begins after tariffs disappear.**
cards.hint: The invisible barriers — a bottle-shape rule, a test certificate.

cards.front: Name the **four freedoms** of the single market — the concrete rights it turns "one market" into.
cards.back:
Free movement of **① Goods** (sell products across borders) · **② Services** (provide services across borders) · **③ Capital** (move & invest across borders) · **④ People / labour** (move, work & establish businesses).

*Crucially they are* **not equally complete**: **goods** furthest along, **capital** freed early, **labour** held back by qualifications, **services** the least complete.
cards.hint: G-S-C-P — the backbone of the lecture.

cards.front: Which freedom is the **model / template** for the whole market — furthest along — and by what device was it solved?
cards.back:
**Free movement of GOODS.**

Solved by the **"new approach"**: **mutual recognition** by default (a product legal in one state is legal in all) + **minimum EU harmonization** *only* on health & safety.

The **1985 White Paper** attacked three barriers to goods: **physical** (border checks), **fiscal** (VAT/excise — only partly done), **technical** (product standards — the hard one).
cards.hint: You can ship it in a box.

cards.front: How does the **"new approach" to standards** let the EU free the movement of goods **without harmonizing everything**? Trace it to the **CE mark**.
cards.back:
**① Default rule = mutual recognition** — a product lawfully marketed in one state is legal in all → no need to harmonize every rule.
**② Exception = health & safety** — for these the EU sets **minimum standards** via the standards bodies **CEN / CENELEC**.
**③** A product meeting them earns the **"CE" mark** and **can't be barred anywhere.**

*Still patchy* where **no harmonized standard exists** — extra national tests appear "especially in **France and Germany**," and **public procurement** rarely goes to non-national firms.
cards.hint: Mutual recognition + minimum H&S standards → a stamp.

cards.front: Free movement of **persons** was extended beyond workers — to whom? And what remains the **main barrier** to real labour mobility?
cards.back:
The **1985 White Paper** extended residence rights to the **economically inactive** — **students, the retired, the unemployed** — with **non-discrimination** in social & welfare benefits.

**Main barrier:** **non-recognition of professional & educational qualifications** — a nurse or architect qualified in one state may not be recognized in another.

The welfare tension it raises (whose wage/welfare rules apply across a border?) explodes in the **Services Directive**.
cards.hint: Not just workers — and a qualifications problem.

cards.front: Which freedom "**had already started to disappear**" as a barrier and was largely freed early by the White Paper — and what remains its unfinished business?
cards.back:
**Free movement of CAPITAL.**

The White Paper freed cross-border **securities, loans, and access to foreign stock exchanges** (three directives).

**Unfinished:** integrating capital *markets* — the **Financial Services Action Plan (1999)** and, under Juncker, the **Capital Markets Union** (emulate the US, channel savings into **SMEs**, offset eurozone states' constrained fiscal capacity after the crisis).
cards.hint: Money and investment — the early winner.

cards.front: Distinguish the **two ways to build an integrated market** — the lecture's central analytical tool. Who is the chief agent of each?
cards.back:
**Negative integration** = **remove barriers** — prohibit discrimination, strike down restrictions, challenge national rules. **Chief agent: the CJEU** (courts remove barriers, e.g. *Cassis*).

**Positive integration** = **create common rules (harmonization)** — common standards, regulations, institutions & enforcement. **Chief agents: Commission + Council + EP** (legislation).

The EU uses **both** — integration means *taking rules away* **and** *making rules at EU level.*
cards.hint: Remove vs create; court vs legislature.

cards.front: ***Cassis de Dijon* (1979):** Germany blocked a French blackcurrant liqueur for failing its **minimum-alcohol** rule. What did the CJEU do, what principle did it establish, and why is it the engine of **negative integration**?
cards.back:
The CJEU **struck the barrier down** and established **mutual recognition**: a product **lawfully marketed in one member state** should generally be **allowed onto the market of another.**

**Why it matters:** the Court **actively removed a barrier** to free movement of goods — **integration through law**, with *no new legislation*. The Court didn't just settle a dispute; it **defined what market integration requires.**
cards.hint: A liqueur that wrote the rulebook — mutual recognition.

cards.front: **Harmonization** vs **mutual recognition** — two strategies for the same goal (stop national rules fragmenting the market). Pros and cons of each?
cards.back:
**Harmonization** — **replace** different national rules with **common EU rules.** *Pro:* a genuine level playing field. *Con:* slow, politically hard, one-size-fits-all.

**Mutual recognition** — **keep** national rules, but each state **recognizes** goods/services meeting **another** state's rules. *Pro:* fast, respects diversity. *Con:* fear of a **"race to the bottom"** — whoever regulates most loosely wins.
cards.hint: Replace the rules vs recognize each other's.

cards.front: The SEM stalled in the 1970s ("**eurosclerosis**"). How did the **1992 relaunch** finally deliver it — and why did it need **both an idea and a way to decide**?
cards.back:
**The idea — "Project 1992":** the **1985 Delors Commission** → the **Cockfield White Paper** listing **~279 measures** to remove remaining barriers → a hard deadline: **31 December 1992.**

**The way to decide — the Single European Act (1987):** expanded **Qualified Majority Voting** for market laws, so single-market measures could **no longer be vetoed** by one state.

→ The market needed not just an economic plan but a **way of making collective decisions** — which is why the SEA mattered so much.
cards.hint: Cockfield's checklist + SEA's QMV.

cards.front: **Why are services so much harder to integrate than goods?** (By 2005 only ~20% of services were traded across borders.)
cards.back:
Because **a service is often inseparable from the person or organization providing it** — you can't ship it in a box.

Providing a service across a border often needs **people, professional qualifications, local licences, establishment abroad, and interaction with national regulators**, plus far more **information asymmetry / trust.**

This is exactly why the **Services Directive** became a political firestorm.
cards.hint: You can't put a haircut or legal advice in a box.

cards.front: The core services dilemma: **home-country (country-of-origin)** vs **host-country** rules. A Polish firm wins a temporary job in Denmark — whose rules govern it, and what's the trade-off?
cards.back:
**Home-country / country-of-origin** — the firm operates under **its own (Polish) rules.** *Frictionless*, but risks a **"race to the bottom."**
**Host-country** — the firm must meet **Denmark's** requirements. *Protects standards*, but **re-fragments the market.**

**The master question:** *which country should regulate cross-border economic activity?* This exact fight is what the **Services Directive** was about.
cards.hint: Frictionless but risky vs protective but fragmenting.

cards.front: The EU liberalized service sectors **one at a time**. Contrast **telecommunications** with **energy** — why was one easier than the other?
cards.back:
**Telecoms — relatively successful:** helped by **US deregulation pressure** and **business lobbying.**

**Energy — harder:** the **"public service argument"**, French defence of **EdF / Gaz de France**, and **union job fears.**

Both show services being prised open **sector by sector**, often over **national-monopoly resistance** — you can't just declare services free the way you (roughly) can with goods.
cards.hint: One had US pressure behind it; the other guarded national champions.

cards.front: The **Services Directive** went "**from Frankenstein to toothless vampire.**" Trace the proposal (2004) → the explosion → the dilution (2006).
cards.back:
**Proposal (2004):** Commissioner **Bolkestein** proposed a single market in services built on the **country-of-origin principle** — firms operate abroad under **home-country rules** (a *Cassis* mutual-recognition move for services).

**Explosion:** it raised the spectre of **"social dumping"** after the **2004 eastern enlargement** — the **"Polish plumber"**, the Swedish **Laval** case. **Unions mobilized**; France dubbed it the **"Frankenstein directive"** (pun on Bolke-*stein*); it tangled with the **2005 French & Dutch referendums.**

**Dilution (adopted 12 Dec 2006, EP 394–215–33):** **country-of-origin removed** → vaguer **"freedom to provide services"**; **host-country labour law preserved**; whole **sectors excluded** (healthcare, gambling, temp agencies, transport, postal…); a **screening system** added.
cards.hint: Country-of-origin proposed → gutted into a toothless clause.

cards.front: **Why was the Services Directive watered down?** Give Jensen & Nedergaard's **actor-centred rational-choice institutionalist** explanation — the four moving parts.
cards.back:
**① The German pivot:** the new **grand coalition (CDU/CSU–SPD, Nov 2005)** used ties to *both* big EP groups (EPP & PES, both German-led) to broker a **lowest-common-denominator** text — pre-empting **Council** opposition.
**② Interest-group asymmetry (Olson):** **unions won the framing war** (concentrated costs → mobilize); **consumers** (diffuse gains) didn't organize. States with the *most* barriers opposed *most*.
**③ Two-level games (Putnam) + "shadow of QMV":** France/Germany pointed to **small win-sets** (referendum/election pressure); the deal was struck **in the shadow of the vote** (a credible blocking minority). CEE states had **large win-sets** → took the low denominator, won the **screening system** as a bargaining chip.
**④ Endogenous preferences:** the constitutional crisis itself pushed everyone toward compromise.

*Prima facie the **EP** was decisive (it wrote the text) — but the real drivers were bargaining & interests.*
cards.hint: German brokerage · Olson · Putnam · reshaped preferences.

cards.front: Name the folk-devil term: **firms from low-wage member states undercutting high-wage states by importing their cheaper home rules** — the fear that detonated the Services Directive.
cards.back:
**Social dumping.**

Its folk-devils: the French **"Polish plumber" (*le plombier polonais*)**, Polish workers in German slaughterhouses, the Swedish **Laval** case. Bulmer's vivid image: a **British firm building a house in Germany with British workers on British terms.**

The fear became acute after the **2004 eastern enlargement** and helped sink the **2005 Constitution referendums.**
cards.hint: The Polish plumber personified it.

cards.front: Define a **posted worker** — and explain why a single posting creates a **governance knot**.
cards.back:
A **posted worker** = "an employee **temporarily sent** by an employer to another EU member state to provide a service."

**The knot:** one posting tangles **three rule-systems** at once — **home-country employment relationship** + **host-country workplace** + **EU free-movement rules.** *Which rules apply, and who enforces them?*

This is the **unresolved remainder** of the services fight.
cards.hint: Temporarily sent abroad — three rulebooks collide.

cards.front: **The Laval / Vaxholm case (2007):** a Latvian firm renovated a Swedish school using Latvian workers on Latvian pay; Swedish unions blockaded the site. How did the CJEU rule, and why was it a shock?
cards.back:
The **CJEU sided (largely) with the firm's freedom to provide services** over the unions' collective action.

**Shock** to **Nordic wage-setting**, which relies on **collective bargaining**, not statutory minimum wages. With ***Viking***, it's the classic proof that **market freedoms can trump national labour rights.**

Sharpest evidence for **Scharpf's** thesis: **negative integration beats positive** — the Court can strike down social protections faster than the EU can legislate them.
cards.hint: Freedom to provide services > Nordic collective bargaining.

cards.front: Trace the EU's response on posting — the shift from **"market opening" to "fair mobility."**
cards.back:
**Posting of Workers Directive (1996)** → **Enforcement Directive (2014)** → **2018 revision** strengthening **host-country pay** ("**equal pay for equal work in the same place**") and distinguishing **short- vs long-term** postings.

Posted workers **help firms fill short-term skill shortages** (esp. construction, border regions) — **but cross-border enforcement is genuinely hard** (different rules, monitoring difficulties, abuse risk).
cards.hint: 1996 → 2014 → 2018, drifting toward host-country pay.

cards.front: How does an integrated market **change the role of the state** — from what it *could* decide **before** to what constrains it **after**?
cards.back:
**Before:** a government could largely decide **who enters** the market, **which standards** apply, **which firms get support**, **which services are protected.**

**After:** those decisions are constrained by EU **free-movement** rules, EU **competition** rules, **common standards**, and **CJEU case law + EU state-aid rules.**

The state doesn't disappear — it turns from **gatekeeper** into **rule-taker.** The deep stakes: the single market **relocates decisions** from national to European level (and to courts & regulators).
cards.hint: Gatekeeper → rule-taker.

cards.front: The single market keeps **re-opening** as the economy changes. Sketch its evolution **beyond the crisis into the digital age.**
cards.back:
**After the eurozone crisis (2009):** intra-EU trade dropped, reviving fears of **economic nationalism** → the **Monti report (2010)** → **Single Market Act I (2011) & II (2012).**

**Juncker era:** **Capital Markets Union**; the **Digital Single Market** (mobile **roaming charges abolished, 2017**); a **"Better Regulation"** agenda.

**Today — digital markets:** the problem has moved from tariffs/product rules to **platforms, data, network effects** → the **Digital Markets Act (DMA)**, **Digital Services Act (DSA)**, and **AI Act**, backed by competition policy.
cards.hint: Monti → Single Market Acts → DMA/DSA/AI Act (roaming died 2017).

cards.front: **Is the single market "neoliberal"?** Contrast **Majone's** pro-market view with the **critical political-economy** view (Scharpf; Cafruny & Ryner; van Apeldoorn).
cards.back:
**Majone (pro-market):** the SEM makes the EU a **"regulatory state."** Delegating regulation to **"non-majoritarian" institutions** (Commission, courts, agencies) **maximizes efficiency** — a welfare good. On this **"output legitimacy"** view, the EU has **no democratic deficit.**

**Critical view:** the SEM embeds a **US-led neoliberal turn** — privatization, welfare retrenchment, liberalized corporate governance — often at business's bidding (the **ERT**). It erodes Europe's social models.
cards.hint: Regulatory-state efficiency vs neoliberal erosion.

cards.front: **"Market-making races ahead while market-correcting rules lag, because the Court can strike down national social protections but the EU struggles to legislate a Social Europe in their place."** Whose thesis, and what's it called?
cards.back:
**Scharpf** — the **structural asymmetry** between **negative and positive integration.**

**Market-making** (negative — courts, mutual recognition) is *strong*; **market-correcting** (positive — a common social floor, **"Social Europe"**) is *weak*, because the **CJEU can strike down** national social protections (**Laval, Viking, 2007**) faster than the EU can build EU-level replacements.

*Great exam hinge:* link this straight back to the **negative/positive integration** distinction.
cards.hint: Negative beats positive — Social Europe lags.

cards.front: Two more positions in the neoliberal debate: (a) both sides **overstate the structural imperatives**; the market is contestable and diverse — and (b) **popular dissatisfaction may brake further integration.** Name each.
cards.back:
**(a) Constructivist middle — Hay & Wincott:** the market is **not fully "depoliticized"** — it's contestable (witness the Services Directive), some CJEU rulings **protected** national prerogatives, and **welfare-capitalist diversity persists.**

**(b) Postfunctionalism:** **popular dissatisfaction** with the EU can act as a **brake** on further market integration. *(It went political in the UK — "**Lexiteers**" argued the single market forces neoliberalism on Britain: a left-wing case for Brexit.)*
cards.hint: The middle ground vs the mass-politics brake.

cards.front: The capstone question: is the single market built by **states pursuing interests (LI)** or by **supranational entrepreneurship & spillover (neofunctionalism)**? Apply both to **Project 1992**, **Cassis**, and the **Services Directive**.
cards.back:
| Episode | **LI** | **Neofunctionalism** |
|---|---|---|
| **Project 1992** | changing national **preferences** + interstate **bargaining** (FR/DE/UK converge) | **Commission entrepreneurship** (Delors, ERT) + momentum |
| **Cassis** | states **built the legal framework** the Court works in | the **CJEU** drives integration through **supranational action** |
| **Services Directive** | domestic **preferences + bargaining** (German-brokered deal) | supranational **ambition meets resistance** (Commission overreached) |
cards.hint: States bargaining vs Commission/Court pushing.

cards.front: Pull it together: **is the single market economics or politics** — and what's the honest verdict on which integration theory wins?
cards.back:
The **red thread:** the single market is an **institutional & political project**, not an automatic economic one — it develops through **political bargaining** (the Services Directive proves it) and it **changes the role of the state** from gatekeeper to rule-taker.

**On theory — no single one wins.** Bulmer's map: the *original common market* fits **LI**; the *1960 acceleration* looked **neofunctionalist**; *1992* is genuinely **contested** (Delors/ERT vs Moravcsik's member-state mandate); the *post-1992 momentum* is best read as **historical institutionalism** (the SEA changed the rules; the CJEU entrenched free-market readings).

**Verdict:** *states set the frame, but courts, the Commission and institutional momentum keep pushing it further than any single bargain intended.*
cards.hint: Politics not just economics; no theory wins outright.
